original_parent_fields.label: Sans-culottes as a political movement and moral economy
original_parent_fields.meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Ordinary artisans and tradesmen claimed a political identity, drove demonstrations and insurrection, demanded vengeance, participated in massacres, volunteered for war, and pressured representative institutions. Organized Parisian popular militants claim guardianship of the Republic, press economic demands, and supply the coercive strength behind political purges. Sansculottes defended a moral economy, popular democracy, and suspicion of wealth and expertise that conflicted with the market liberalism and property priorities of 1789; after serving revolutionary governments, they were suppressed and left without gains.
original_parent_fields.stance: Preserve the combined source qualifications: The movement is socially and politically consequential but not homogeneous; its members' beliefs and actions are explained without endorsing violence. Their power is indispensable to the Republic yet volatile, internally divided, and capable of subordinating representative government. In relation to the founding liberal programme, sansculotte resistance can itself be called anti-revolutionary, despite its familiar status as the paradigm of popular revolution.
